analysis.one_liner: Offers Senate candidates public campaign funds if they rely on small donations and caps large donations.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in December 2022 and sent to the Finance Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 — it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a voluntary public financing system for Senate campaigns. Candidates who show broad small-dollar support (thousands of donations of $5–$200 from people in their state) could receive public grants, matching payments of up to 600% of each small donation, and TV ad vouchers. In exchange, they would accept no large donations — individual contributions capped at $1,000 — no joint fundraising with party committees, and only $50,000 of personal money. The fund would be paid for by a 0.5% tax on payments under federal contracts worth more than $10 million.
analysis.who_benefits: Senate candidates who can build support from many small donors rather than a few large ones, and voters who want candidates unencumbered by big-donor and special-interest money. Public grant amounts scale with state size ($750,000 plus $150,000 per congressional district), and leftover public funds must be returned.

how_it_helps.text: Participating candidates receive a public allocation ($750,000 plus $150,000 per congressional district for the general election), a 600% match on small-dollar contributions capped at 400% of their allocation, an additional enhanced payment, and broadcast advertising vouchers of $100,000 per congressional district. [S3]

In exchange, participating candidates may accept contributions from individuals only up to $1,000 per election, may not form joint fundraising committees, and may use at most $50,000 of personal or immediate-family funds — reducing candidates' dependence on large donors. [S3]
Candidates must qualify with a minimum of 2,000 contributions of $5–$200 (plus 500 per congressional district) from residents of their state, tying public funds to broad grassroots support. [S3]
Unspent public money must be remitted back to the fund within 180 days after the election, except limited amounts carried into a runoff or the next cycle under certification. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Companies holding federal contracts worth more than $10 million, which would pay a 0.5% tax on contract payments capped at $500,000 per contract per year. Large donors, joint fundraising committees, and the political parties' big-check fundraising operations would also see their role in Senate campaigns shrink for participating candidates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large federal contractors and big donors

drawbacks.text: The program is funded by a tax on large government contracts, which is generally passed through to taxpayers and consumers through contract prices and bids. [S3]

The bill applies only to Senate elections and only to candidates who opt in; non-participating candidates, outside groups, and super PAC spending would remain unlimited, so the program would not touch the dominant channels of campaign money. [S3]

The grant and match amounts are fixed formulas that may fall short of what competitive Senate races actually cost, especially in large media markets; the bill directs the FEC to review adequacy after each election but does not guarantee adjustments. [S3]

The Congressional Revenue provisions rely partly on a 'sense of the Senate' rather than a mandatory appropriation, so funding of the program could depend on future Congresses choosing to appropriate the contract-tax revenue. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is a Senate campaign finance channel that doesn't depend on large individual, corporate, or joint-fundraising money, at the cost of a new tax on very large federal contracts. The main design weakness is that it is voluntary and Senate-only, so unlimited outside spending and non-participating candidates would still exist; whether public amounts are adequate for real Senate races is untested. The bill died before any committee or floor debate, so none of these tradeoffs was ever tested in a public hearing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on December 15, 2022, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee. It stayed there until the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the Fair Elections Now Act of 2022 in the Senate on December 15, 2022, with eight Democratic and one Independent co-sponsor. [S1] [S4]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action was taken. [S5]
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died in committee and all its provisions lapsed. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large federal contractors are better off because the 0.5% contract tax was never enacted, and candidates and parties that rely on large-dollar fundraising and joint fundraising committees are better off because the program that would have restricted them never started.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large federal contractors and big-money fundraisers

for.name: 8 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate Independents
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sen. Sanders (I-VT), Sens. Markey, Murphy, Klobuchar, Smith, Schatz, and Warren

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the Senate Finance Committee (Chair: Sen. Ron Wyden, D-OR)
against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was referred took no action — no hearing or markup — for the three weeks remaining in the Congress. [S5]

against.name: Senate Majority Leader
against.role: Senate Majority Leader (Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 50 Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill, and no Republican-supported version advanced. [S4]

sides.party_line_note: All 10 sponsors were Democrats or allied Independents; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and it died in a committee controlled by the Democratic majority in the Senate's final days.

industries.note: The bill would impose a 0.5% tax on payments under federal contracts over $10 million (capped at $500,000 per contract per year) to fund the program, and that cost is typically built into contract prices paid by taxpayers. Because the bill died, contractors keep the status quo.

The bill would require stations to accept government-issued advertising vouchers, creating a new guaranteed payment stream for political airtime while giving candidates publicly funded ad dollars. Stations would gain revenue but lose discretion over what payment forms they accept.

industries.industry: Large-donor fundraising infrastructure (joint fundraising committees, party committees' big-dollar operations)
industries.note: Participating candidates would be barred from joint fundraising committees and capped at $1,000 per individual donor, shrinking the role of big-check fundraising in Senate campaigns. Because the bill never advanced, these operations are unchanged.
